blogs.title: When Prior Possession Becomes Evidence: Rule 404(b) and Felon‑in‑Possession Cases in the Eighth Circuit
blogs.description: This post examines how the Cutbank opinion treats witnesses’ testimony about prior sightings of a sawed‑off rifle as “intrinsic” rather than prohibited propensity evidence under Rule 404(b). It dissects the Battle precedent relied upon by the panel, compares approaches taken by other circuits, and evaluates the policy tension between proving continuous firearm ownership and preventing unfair character attacks. The article will consider whether the Eighth Circuit’s reasoning signals a shift toward broader admissibility of prior possession evidence in felon‑in‑possession prosecutions.

blogs.title: Victim Statements, Hearsay, and the Confrontation Clause: The Eighth Circuit’s Approach in United States v. Cutbank
blogs.description: Focusing on D.F.’s pre‑trial statements to police, this analysis explores whether a limiting instruction was required to satisfy Confrontation Clause concerns. It reviews key precedents such as Charboneau and Bennett, clarifies when out‑of‑court statements become admissible through “available witness” or “statement against interest” doctrines, and assesses whether cutting off such evidence would affect a jury’s factual findings in violent crime cases. The piece also reflects on broader trends in handling victim testimony across federal courts.

blogs.title: Stacking Sentencing Enhancements Under the ACCA and USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B): Does Cutbank’s Sentence Meet the ‘Sufficient but Not Greater Than Necessary’ Standard?
blogs.description: The article breaks down the district court’s calculation of a 35 offense level—four separate enhancements including saw‑off firearms, serial‑number alteration, reckless flight risk, and possession in connection with another felony—and its interaction with mandatory ACCA penalties. It analyzes statutory language in § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B), relevant commentary (n.14(C)), and precedent such as Dunn to determine whether cumulative enhancements violate § 3553(a)’s core principle that sentences be no greater than necessary. The discussion also touches on post‑Booker advisory guideline theory.

blogs.title: Harmless Error Doctrine After Eighth Circuit Trial Rulings: Lessons from United States v. Cutbank
blogs.description: This post reviews how appellate courts assess alleged evidentiary errors under DeMarce and Keys, focusing on Cutbank’s claim that trial‑court rulings were prejudicial. It explains what constitutes “substantial prejudice” versus a harmless mistake, why the panel found no reversible error despite multiple objections raised by defense counsel, and what this tells us about deference to trial judges in criminal cases. The piece concludes with implications for future defendants seeking relief based on trial‑court evidentiary rulings.
